Empirical Research Plan  
“How does the presence of hazardous waste sites affect housing market outcomes? What is the impact of the Superfund program on property values in areas surrounding these sites?”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DID) implemented as a staggered-adoption event-study.  

Why appropriate  
• The “treatment” (listing/cleanup under the Superfund program) occurs at different sites in different years between 1980-2000 → classic staggered policy adoption.  
• We observe repeated cross-sections (or a balanced panel) of census-tract housing values before and after treatment.  
• Parallel-trend assumption can be interrogated with pre-period event-time coefficients.  

Supplemental robustness: Fuzzy Regression-Discontinuity (RDD) that instruments for Superfund listing with the site’s Hazard Ranking System (HRS) score relative to the 28.5 cutoff for placement on the National Priorities List (NPL). The DID is the work-horse; the RDD serves as a check.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
T_it = 1 if census tract i’s centroid lies within 1 mile of a hazardous waste site j that is ever listed on the NPL and year t is ≥ the site’s listing year (or ≥ the cleanup-completion year in an alternative spec). Otherwise 0.

Control group (counterfactual) – Two layers  
A. Spatial counterfactual: Tracts 1–3 miles from the same site (or from other CERCLIS sites that never enter Superfund) give us “near but not too near” properties that share local labor-market and amenity shocks.  
B. Temporal counterfactual: For treated tracts, pre-listing (or pre-cleanup) years serve as own comparison.

Treatment timing / event date  
Event date τ_j: year in which site j is formally listed on the NPL (τ_j^list) or the year cleanup is certified complete (τ_j^clean).  
Event-time dummies k = −10,…,+10 are coded relative to τ_j.

Running variable & cutoff (for the RDD robustness)  
Running variable: HRS score ∈ [0, 100] assigned during site inspection.  
Cutoff: 28.5 (sites ≥ 28.5 are eligible for NPL). The RDD is fuzzy because some high-score sites still avoid listing and vice-versa.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel Trends (DID): Absent Superfund listing, housing values in tracts within 1 mile and 1–3 miles of CERCLIS sites would evolve similarly.  
• Plausibility: Both sets of tracts share the same counties, school districts, labor markets. Can be evaluated with pre-treatment event-time coefficients.

A2. No Differential Concurrent Policies: No other place-specific shocks coincide systemically with Superfund listing.  
• EPA listing is mainly driven by site toxicity, not by local development policies, suggesting plausibility once we include site-fixed effects and county×year FEs.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (No Spillovers): Clean-up of site j affects only the “near” tracts we code as treated, not farther tracts.  
• Some spillovers <3 mi are possible; we will test different rings (0–1, 1–3, 3–5 miles) to show treated vs. control is sufficiently separated.

A4. No Selective Migration that Changes Composition Differentially in Response to Anticipation.  
• We can use decennial census tract fixed effects and check whether tract population or housing stock changes sharply pre-listing.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Violation of Parallel Trends  
• Test: Plot event-study coefficients for k ≤ −3; include tract-specific linear trends; propensity-score re-weight so pre-period trends match.

T2. Anticipation / Announcement Effects  
• Use announcement year instead of listing year in alternative timing; include leads in event study and interpret upward pre-trend as anticipation; if large, re-define treatment beginning two years before listing.

T3. Spatial Spillovers / General Equilibrium Effects  
• Estimate models with multiple rings (0–1, 1–3, 3–5 miles).  
• Cluster SEs at the site level to account for spatial correlation.  
• Exclude multi-site counties as robustness.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# Required packages --------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)        # fast high-dimensional FE
library(lubridate)
library(rdrobust)      # robustness RDD
library(modelsummary)  # nice tables

# 1. Data loading -----------------------------------------------------
tract   <- read_csv("census_tract_panel_1980_2000.csv")   # tract-year data
sites   <- read_csv("cerclis_sites.csv")                  # site-level info incl. coords, HRS, NPL year
distmat <- read_csv("tract_site_distances.csv")           # pre-calculated tract-to-site distances

# 2. Merge and variable construction --------------------------------
# nearest site to each tract
nearest <- distmat %>% group_by(tract_id, year) %>%
  arrange(distance_mi) %>% slice(1) %>% ungroup()

panel <- tract %>%
  left_join(nearest, by = c("tract_id","year")) %>%
  left_join(sites %>% 
              select(site_id, npl_year, cleanup_year, hrs_score), 
            by = "site_id") %>%
  mutate(within1 = (distance_mi<=1),
         near13  = (distance_mi>1 & distance_mi<=3),
         treat_post = if_else(within1 & year >= npl_year, 1, 0, missing = 0),
         event_time = year - npl_year,
         log_price = log(median_value))

# 3. Main DID specification -----------------------------------------
did_main <- feols(log_price ~ treat_post + pct_owner_occ + median_income |
                    tract_id + year, 
                  cluster = ~site_id, 
                  data = panel %>% filter(within1 | near13))

summary(did_main)

# 4. Event-study (Sun & Abraham) ------------------------------------
event <- feols(log_price ~ sunab(npl_year, year, ref = -1) + pct_owner_occ + median_income |
                 tract_id + year,
               cluster = ~site_id,
               data    = panel %>% filter(within1 | near13))

iplot(event, ci_level = .95, ref.line = 0)

# 5. Robustness check: RD around HRS 28.5 ----------------------------
# restrict to observations with hrs in [15, 45]
rd_data <- sites %>% filter(hrs_score >= 15 & hrs_score <= 45) %>%
           mutate(listed = if_else(!is.na(npl_year),1,0))

rd_out <- rdrobust(y = rd_data$listed, x = rd_data$hrs_score, c = 28.5)
summary(rd_out)

# 6. Store results ---------------------------------------------------
modelsummary(list(did_main, event), stars = TRUE, gof_omit = 'Adj')
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic intuition: Unremediated hazardous sites depress nearby property values via health risk and disamenity. Cleanup (or credible commitment to future cleanup) should raise prices. Prior literature finds 4–11 percent increases within 2 km. I expect:  

β_DID ≈ +0.05 to +0.07 in logs → 5–7 percent increase in median house value within 1 mile after listing/cleanup, relative to 1–3 mile tracts.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable/absent)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Evidence of parallel pre-trends (visual + joint F-test) ........ 1  
C2: No contemporaneous confounders / policy bundles ................ 0.5  
C3: Correct treatment timing & no anticipation bias ................ 0.5  
C4: No interference across units (spillovers) ...................... 0.5  
C5: Stable unit composition (no differential migration) ............ 0.5  

Total ≈ 3/5. While plausible, we must document pre-trends and spillover robustness to strengthen credibility.
